title: Primary and foreign keys
objectives: Explain how keys link two tables
Tell a primary key from a foreign key, including a key of two columns
Follow a foreign key with a subquery in `WHERE`

screens.title: Two tables, one question
screens.prose: A database splits its facts into tables. `securities` holds one row per company. `prices` holds closing prices, here for 4 March 2026. Neither table on its own says which closes belong to energy companies.

state.caption: prices on 4 March (the date column is left out)

screens.question: Tap the ticker of every price row that belongs to an Energy company.

hints.text: Which companies does `securities` list as Energy?
BP and Shell are the Energy companies. Shell trades under the ticker SHEL.
Find BP and SHEL in the ticker column of `prices` and tap both.

feedback.correct: BP and SHEL. You matched each price to its company through the ticker.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look each sector up in `securities`, then find those tickers in `prices`.

byKey.r0c0: AZN is AstraZeneca, listed under Health. Read the sector from the left table.
byKey.r1c0: BARC is Barclays, a bank. Read the sector from the left table.
byKey.r3c0: HSBA is HSBC, a bank. Read the sector from the left table.
byKey.r5c0: VOD is Vodafone, listed under Telecoms. Read the sector from the left table.
byKey.r2c0: You missed BP. The left table lists BP under Energy.
byKey.r4c0: You missed SHEL. Shell is an Energy company, and its ticker is SHEL.

explain.text: You read each sector in one table and found the matching tickers in the other. The `ticker` column is what links the two tables. A column that links tables like this is called a **key**.

screens.title: Why not one big table?
screens.prose: Here is the same data as one wide table. Every price row repeats the company name and sector. It shows BP and Shell over three days.
screens.question: Shell renames itself Shell plc. How many rows of this table must change?

widget.label: Rows to change
widget.accept: 3: every Shell row carries the name.

hints.text: Which rows mention Shell?
The name sits in every Shell row.
Count the rows whose name is Shell.

feedback.correct: Three rows, one per day, each repeating the name.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rows that say Shell.

byKey.once: You changed one row. The other two Shell rows would still say Shell, so the table would contradict itself.
byKey.all: Only the Shell rows carry its name. The BP rows stay as they are.

explain.text: Every Shell price row repeats the name, so all 3 must change; five years of prices would mean 1,260. In the split design the name sits once in `securities`, so one row changes. Store each fact once and link the rest by key.

screens.title: The primary key
screens.prose: Back to the split tables. A **primary key** is a column whose value picks out exactly one row. It is never empty and never repeats within its table.
screens.question: Which column is the primary key of `securities`?

options.why: You picked the name. Names change, as Shell's just did, and a key has to stay fixed.
Banks appears twice, so a sector cannot pick out one company.

options.text: None of them: any column could repeat
options.why: Each company has one ticker and no two share it. That is exactly what a primary key needs.

hints.text: Which column has a different value on every row?
Look down the sector column: Banks appears twice.
Only `ticker` is different on every row and is fixed for each company.

feedback.correct: Each ticker appears once, so it picks out one company.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the column that never repeats.

byKey.sector: Banks appears twice in `sector`. A key value must pick out a single row.

explain.text: Each ticker appears once in `securities`, so it picks out one company. Other tables refer to a company by its ticker, never by its name.

screens.title: The same column, another table
screens.prose:
`prices` has a `ticker` column too. Here are its rows for BP and Shell.

```sql
SELECT close FROM prices
WHERE ticker = 'BP';
```
screens.question: How many rows does this query return?

options.why: You treated `ticker` as the key of `prices`. BP has one price row per day, so the ticker repeats here.
That counts Shell as well. The `WHERE` keeps only the BP rows.

options.text: An error: `ticker` is the key of another table
options.why: A column can be a key in one table and an ordinary column in another. The query runs.

hints.text: How many BP rows can you see?
BP has a row for each of the three days.
One BP close per day for three days gives 3 rows.

feedback.correct: One BP row per day: 3 rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the BP rows in `prices`.

byKey.one: You treated `ticker` as the key of `prices`. It is unique in `securities`, but here BP has one row per day.

explain.text: `ticker` is unique in `securities` but repeats in `prices`, once per day. In `prices` it points at a company in another table: it is a **foreign key**. It is not the key of `prices` itself.

screens.title: A key made of two columns
screens.prose: So what picks out one row of `prices`? A primary key can be two columns taken together.
screens.question: Which pair of columns picks out exactly one row of `prices`?

options.why: A stock can close at the same price on two different days, so that pair can repeat.
Two companies can close at the same price on the same day, so that pair can repeat.
Six companies share every date, so the date alone repeats six times.

hints.text: Which two facts together fix one close?
One company has exactly one close on each day.
A ticker with a date names one close, and that pair can never repeat.

feedback.correct: One company, one day, one close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the pair that can never repeat.

explain.text: One company has one close per day, so the pair `(ticker, date)` never repeats. That pair is the primary key of `prices`, and the schema says so with `PRIMARY KEY (ticker, date)`.

screens.title: A key with nothing behind it
screens.prose:
`prices.ticker` refers to `securities.ticker`. A data feed now adds this row for Lloyds:

```sql
INSERT INTO prices
VALUES ('LLOY', '2026-03-04', 0.52);
```

`LLOY` has no row in `securities`.
screens.question: What is wrong with the new row?

options.why: SQLite stores it, but the link is broken. Any lookup of its sector finds nothing.

options.text: SQLite refuses it because LLOY is missing
options.why: Only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. SQLite does not check foreign keys by default, so this row goes in.
No LLOY row exists for 4 March yet, so the pair (LLOY, 2026-03-04) is new.

hints.text: Where would a query find Lloyds's sector?
The foreign key should match a ticker in `securities`.
`LLOY` matches no row in `securities`, so the link leads nowhere.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the ticker into `securities`.

byKey.refused: You expected SQLite to check the link. It does so only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`; by default the row goes in.

explain.text: A foreign key with no matching row is an **orphan**. SQLite rejects orphans only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`, so data from a feed needs checking. Later in this level you will find orphans with a query.

screens.title: A query inside a query
screens.prose:
One query can use the answer of another. The query in brackets runs first and hands its rows to `IN`.

```sql
SELECT ticker, close FROM prices
WHERE date = '2026-03-04'
  AND ticker IN (SELECT ticker
                 FROM securities
                 WHERE sector = 'Banks');
```
screens.question: Which list does the inner query hand to `IN`?

options.why: You took the names. The inner query selects `ticker`, so it returns tickers.
`sector = 'Banks'` only filters the rows. The column it returns is `ticker`.
The `WHERE` inside the brackets keeps only the Banks rows.

hints.text: Read the inner query on its own. Which column does it select?
It selects `ticker` from the rows whose sector is Banks.
Banks rows are Barclays and HSBC, with tickers BARC and HSBA.

feedback.correct: The two bank tickers, BARC and HSBA.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the inner query by eye: which column, which rows?

explain.text: The inner query returns the bank tickers, BARC and HSBA. The outer query keeps the 4 March prices whose ticker is in that list: £2.51 and £8.69. This is a **subquery**: the key carries the answer from one table into the other.

import sqlite3

# Write your SQL between the triple quotes.
def query():
    return """
        SELECT ticker, date, close
        FROM prices
        WHERE ticker IN (SELECT ticker FROM securities
                         WHERE sector = 'Energy')
        ORDER BY ticker, date
    """

# The tables. The tests build them the same way.
def make_db():
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.executescript("""

    INSERT INTO securities VALUES

    CREATE TABLE prices (ticker TEXT, date TEXT, close REAL,
                         PRIMARY KEY (ticker, date));
    INSERT INTO prices VALUES
        ('AZN', '2026-03-02', 110.20), ('AZN', '2026-03-03', 111.50),
        ('AZN', '2026-03-04', 109.80), ('BARC', '2026-03-02', 2.48),

screens.title: Declaring keys
screens.prose:
You have now used both kinds of key. `CREATE TABLE` declares them. `REFERENCES` marks a foreign key, and `PRIMARY KEY` the column or columns that pick out one row.

```sql
CREATE TABLE securities (
  ticker TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name   TEXT,
  sector TEXT);
CREATE TABLE prices (
  ticker TEXT REFERENCES securities (ticker),
  date   TEXT,
  close  REAL,
  PRIMARY KEY (ticker, date));
```
screens.question: Which insert does SQLite refuse with this schema, even with foreign-key checks off?

options.text: A second row for BP on 2026-03-04

options.why: The pair (BP, 2026-03-05) is new, so the key does not repeat.
A new ticker is a new key value. Nothing repeats.
That breaks the foreign key, which SQLite checks only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.

feedback.correct: A primary key is always enforced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which rule does SQLite check every time?

explain.text: SQLite always enforces a primary key's uniqueness, so a second BP close for 4 March fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed:` `prices.ticker, prices.date`. Unlike other databases it accepts a `NULL` text key, so write `ticker TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY`. Foreign keys are checked only once you switch them on.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 adds Lloyds as a new bank with one trade. Follow the sector through a subquery instead of listing tickers.

ideas: Each fact lives once, in one table. Tables link through keys instead of repeating data.
A primary key picks out one row: `ticker` in `securities`, the pair `(ticker, date)` in `prices`. A foreign key points at another table's primary key.
A subquery follows a key: `ticker IN (SELECT ticker FROM securities WHERE ...)` turns a sector into tickers.

formula.name: Keys of the price table
formula.note: SQLite always enforces a primary key's uniqueness, but not `NOT NULL` unless you declare it; foreign keys only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.

summary.trap: `ticker` is unique in `securities` but repeats in `prices`: a foreign key is not the key of its own table.

quiz.prose: `trades` has columns `id`, `date`, `ticker` and `qty`. Each trade gets a new `id`, and a ticker can be traded many times.
quiz.question: What is the primary key of `trades`?

options.why: A ticker can be traded many times, so it repeats in `trades`. It is a foreign key here.
Two trades in the same stock on the same day would repeat that pair.
That would allow two different trades to share an id. The id alone already picks out one trade.

feedback.correct: Each trade has its own id.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which column can never repeat?

explain.text: A new id for every trade makes `id` unique, so it is the primary key. `ticker` repeats, and it points at `securities`: a foreign key.

quiz.prose: A feed loads 500 price rows into SQLite with foreign-key checks off. Four of them have tickers that are not in `securities`.
quiz.question: How many of the 500 rows does SQLite store?

widget.label: Rows stored
widget.accept: 500: with checks off, orphans are stored like any other row.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does SQLite check foreign keys by default?

byKey.refused: You expected SQLite to reject the four orphans. It checks foreign keys only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.
byKey.none: Nothing stops the load. The four orphans go in alongside the others.

explain.text: Foreign-key checks are off by default in SQLite, so all 500 rows go in. The four orphans are there, but no company matches them.

quiz.prose:
Using the tables from this lesson:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prices
WHERE ticker IN (SELECT ticker FROM securities
                 WHERE sector <> 'Banks');
```
quiz.question: What number does it return?

widget.label: Count
widget.accept: 12: four non-bank companies, three closes each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the companies the subquery returns, then their price rows.

byKey.companies: That is how many tickers the subquery returns. Each has three price rows.
byKey.banks: That counts the bank rows. `<>` means not equal, so banks are left out.
byKey.all: That counts every price row. The subquery removes the two banks.

explain.text: The subquery returns AZN, BP, SHEL and VOD. Each has three closes in `prices`, so the count is $4 \times 3 = 12$.

quiz.prose: A wide table repeats each company's sector on every daily price row. It holds 2,000 companies and 1,260 days of prices.
quiz.question: A company moves sector. How many rows must change in the wide table, and how many in the split design?

options.why: You changed one row of the wide table. Every one of its 1,260 price rows repeats the sector.
Only the one company moves. Its rows change; the other companies stay put.
In the split design the sector sits once, in `securities`. The prices only hold the ticker.

feedback.correct: Every copy in the wide table, one row in the split design.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does the sector live in each design?

explain.text: The wide table stores the sector once per price row, so 1,260 rows change. The split design stores it once in `securities`, so one row changes, and the prices follow by key.
